transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
President Trump has a well-documented history of making false claims about rigged elections.
But even before vote counting was over last night, he said he will accept the results.
NPR's Miles Parks reports on the possible reasons why.
>> It's obviously harder to do with a loss that is this resounding, right?
There was no red mirage where it looked like Republicans might win early in the night and
Trump was not on the ballot last night.
But also all year in conversations I've had with local officials, it was clear that these
sort of fraud narratives were not catching on with voters in the same way they were a
couple of years ago.
>> President Trump spoke briefly about his party's midterm election losses this morning
while taking reporters on a tour of the under construction White House ballroom.
>> After last night's voter repudiation of President Trump, Republicans now must decide
what they want their party to stand for going forward.
Here's NPR's Mora Eliasson.
>> Donald Trump may be a lame duck, but he's still the dominant figure in his party and
the GOP still stands for whatever Trump wants, at least up until now.
But after last night's wipeout, embracing Trump may not be a good strategy for Republicans.
But another problem for Republicans is that Trump still has a lot of power in Republican
primaries.
And those are the next election every Republican in Congress must face in two years.
Mora Eliasson, NPR News.
>> According to a race call by the Associated Press, Republicans have flipped their first
seat of the midterm elections of party one Texas's 32nd congressional district.
That's the only seat the GOP one of the five that was part of the mid decade redistricting
effort in Texas spurred by President Trump.
In addition to full control of Congress, Democrats will have a majority of state governors for
the first time since 2010.
The party is on track to have at least 28 governor's offices having flipped five so
far.
Two governor's races remain too close to call in Kansas and Alaska.
Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear chairs the Democratic Governors Association.
He says Democratic victories deliver the best map in decades for the party's 2028 presidential
nominee.
Beshear spoke with Kentucky public radio Sylvia Goodman.
>> Beshear says the election shows Americans want their governors to focus on everyday
needs and repudiate cruelty.
>> We will not accept leaders who tell us that our neighbor is the enemy from within
and try to push division between us and people we know, simply because they're members of
another party.
>> He said Americans expect their governors to push back against President Donald Trump
pointing, for example, to Democrat-led lawsuits over rescinded funding.
Beshear is considered a possible contender for Democratic nominee in 2028 and has hinted
at potential ambitions.
For NPR News, I'm Sylvia Goodman in Louisville, Kentucky.
>> And you're listening to NPR News.
The Hong Kong court has sentenced prominent activist Joshua Wong to 10 years in prison.
Wong was handed the sentence Thursday for his second conviction under a China-imposed national
security law, Wong is already serving a prison term on an earlier national security charge
linked to an unofficial primary election in 2020.
Conductor Herbert Blumstedt has died at age 99 with a career spanning more than seven
decades.
He was perhaps the oldest working conductor in history and here's Tom Heisinger reports.
>> Herbert Blumstedt led most of the world's best orchestras, including a 10-year stint
directing the San Francisco Symphony.
Joshua Cosman, former classical music critic for the San Francisco Chronicle, says Blumstedt
inherited an orchestra that was skilled but lacking in discipline.
>> Under his guidance, everything became sharper, cleaner, more crisply focused.
>> Blumstedt was born in 1927 in Springfield, Massachusetts to Swedish parents.
John Cage and Leonard Bernstein were among his teachers, his conducting debut came in
1954.
Retirement is not a question of age, he once said, I love music so much, I can't give up.
And he didn't, Tom Heisinger, NPR News.
>> Following the widespread democratic victories in Tuesday's midterm, stocks are advancing,
shares in Asia mostly higher.
After the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped more than 3%, the S&P 500 closed up 1.6% and
the NASDAQ advanced 1.4%.
I'm Giles Snyder, this is NPR News.

Trump speaks briefly about GOP midterm losses while touring the White House ballroom construction
Republicans must decide party's direction after Democrats' midterm wipeout, with Trump still dominant in primaries
Republicans flip Texas's 32nd congressional district, the only redistricting seat the GOP gains
Democrats set to hold majority of state governors for first time since 2010, Kansas and Alaska unresolved
Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear says Democratic midterm wins set up strong 2028 map
Hong Kong court sentences activist Joshua Wong to 10 years on second national security conviction
Conductor Herbert Blumstedt dies at age 99 after a seven-decade career
Stocks advance after Democratic midterm victories, with the Dow up over 3%
